title: Thinking of materializations for Meaning Atlas

body:
Through looking at the materializations again and speaking to my professor I had to reconsider how I was going about developing Meaning Atlas. I had been spending time figuring out how the expressions would connect and what information was needed because there needs to be a reason for the connections in the tree, and also a way to explain where they came from. My professor had asked me to start with a small number of responses and create something people could try. I was still working through how to organise it and then I had to consider what someone would actually do once the information was there, since being able to open a word and read it does not tell me what they understood. The interest has stayed around cultural expression and how people adapt what they say, the visualisation was how I thought I could give those expressions a place as well as allow people to contribute their own accounts.

An example would be me saying, “Yoh this meal is lekker but shame man I wish I could share this with my mense.” Lekker here expresses how good the food is and shame man includes the sadness of not sharing it, then my mense refers to people I feel close to. There is enjoyment and also missing those people within the same sentence. Explaining it in English requires me to separate those parts and say more about what I mean, and then I would still need to hear what the other person understood to know whether the explanation worked. This is why I wanted the tree to keep the individual accounts, because someone else could use the same expression differently and their explanation should be there as well. What I would add is a way for visitors to write what they think before opening the account and then return to it afterwards. Seeing what changed once they had the context, emotion and intention, or whether they understood it already.

Then I thought about how this could happen between friends through a game, where four people write down expressions they want to use as well as their explanations and possible misinterpretations. Everyone is given the same situation and they talk to each other using those words, then the others guess what they meant from the conversation. After that they give the literal translations and discuss whether saying it that way still carries the feeling, and then the cards are laid out for everyone to match explanations to the expressions. One chance for each at that stage, collecting the explanation if they get it right and moving onto context, emotion and intention. The false cards would be mixed in because I wanted them to think about what could reasonably be misunderstood, and also remember how the expression was used instead of only remembering the translation. Writing the false explanations makes the contributor consider that too. How another person could hear what they said and arrive at something different.

For the layers I wanted people to write or type their expressions and explanations first and then try acting out how they use them without giving the meaning away. The audience guesses and receives clues as they get closer or further from the intended meaning, and their guesses stay visible so they can see what the added information changed. I also wanted to include Google Translate, first with the expression alone and then within a sentence, to see if it helps the communication or makes it more difficult. Someone might have been close from the acting and then change their interpretation after seeing the translation, or the translation could help them understand what the performance did not explain. Then the contributor and listener can compare what each meant and understood, with a printed record they could take home as well. These are still things I need to test, including whether people can follow the game and whether acting gives them enough to work with. Starting with a small tree and paper cards would let me see where the difficulties actually happen before adding more to the forms.
